records.title: About
records.summary: What Our West Valley AZ is and how it works.
records.text: About What Our West Valley AZ is and how it works. Our West Valley AZ is an independent, noncommercial civic information project for Arizona's West Valley. It is not affiliated with the City of Avondale or any other government agency. Why OWVAZ exists Useful local government information is often spread across city websites, budgets, meeting portals, agendas, reports, and other public records. OWVAZ organizes that information around what residents are trying to find and explains it in plain language. Find it. Understand it. Go to the source if you want more. How information is researched OWVAZ takes accuracy seriously and prefers authoritative primary sources such as official government websites, adopted budgets, agendas, minutes, resolutions, contracts, and public records. Important factual claims should be traceable to identifiable evidence. Summaries and explanations are intended to make source material easier to understand, not to replace the underlying records. When an official source or service is available, OWVAZ links residents directly to it. When available evidence does not establish something, OWVAZ aims to identify that limitation rather than fill the gap with an assumption. Editorial independence OWVAZ is independently operated. It is not operated by or on behalf of a city, government agency, political candidate, campaign, political party, or government contractor. The project is noncommercial and is intended to help residents find, understand, and verify information about their communities. Use of artificial intelligence OWVAZ may use artificial intelligence tools to assist with organizing, comparing, summarizing, researching, and presenting information. AI tools may also assist with technical work involved in developing and maintaining the website. AI output is not treated as an authoritative source. Factual claims published by OWVAZ are expected to be supported by underlying records or other identifiable sources, and important claims should be verified against those sources whenever practical. Corrections Accuracy is an ongoing responsibility. When reliable information shows that OWVAZ has published a factual error or that important context is missing, OWVAZ aims to correct or clarify the information. Residents are encouraged to provide corrections and supporting sources through the Contact page. Privacy OWVAZ is designed so residents can use the site without being tracked or profiled by OWVAZ. The current site does not require resident accounts and is designed without advertising, tracking pixels, behavioral analytics, browser or device fingerprinting, or third party social trackers. Site searches run in the resident's browser. Read the OWVAZ Privacy page for details about search, cookies, browser storage, external links, and the site's privacy by design approach.

records.title: Disclaimer
records.summary: Important information about using Our West Valley AZ.
records.text: Disclaimer Important information about using Our West Valley AZ. Our West Valley AZ is an independent, noncommercial civic information project. It is not a government agency, is not affiliated with the City of Avondale or any other government agency, and is not an official government record or service. Last updated: September 8, 2026. Accuracy, sources, interpretation, and verification OWVAZ takes accuracy seriously. Information is researched and organized using public records, official government sources, and other authoritative sources whenever practical. Important factual claims are expected to be supported by identifiable evidence. OWVAZ may summarize, organize, categorize, compare, or explain public records and other source material. Those explanations are not themselves official government records and should be read together with the identified sources when the distinction matters. Reasonable people can sometimes interpret the same record or collection of records differently. OWVAZ aims to distinguish documented facts from interpretation and to identify material uncertainty when the available evidence does not establish a conclusion. AI output is not treated as an authoritative source. Public information can also change after publication. When a current deadline, legal requirement, eligibility determination, or other time sensitive official information matters, residents should confirm the current information with the responsible agency or authoritative source. Proposals, budgets, and public records OWVAZ distinguishes between what public records document and what those records do not establish. A proposal, budget request, appropriation, planned purchase, or similar record does not by itself prove that a project, purchase, policy, system, or deployment was ultimately completed or put into use. When the available public record does not establish a fact, OWVAZ aims to say so rather than fill the gap with an assumption. Completeness OWVAZ works to identify and explain useful public information, but the site may not contain every relevant record, update, event, agency action, or development. The absence of information from OWVAZ should not by itself be treated as evidence that an event, action, record, purchase, decision, or other development did not occur. Inclusion does not imply wrongdoing or endorsement The inclusion or discussion of a person, public official, organization, business, expenditure, contract, technology, proposal, investigation, government action, or public record on OWVAZ does not by itself imply wrongdoing, misconduct, endorsement, criticism, affiliation, or any conclusion beyond what the cited information supports. Likewise, linking to, quoting, or identifying an external person, organization, agency, business, or source does not by itself mean that OWVAZ or its operator endorses or is affiliated with that person or entity. External sources and links OWVAZ links to government agencies, public documents, meeting systems, utilities, and other external sources so residents can review information at its source. OWVAZ does not operate or control those external resources. External websites and documents can change, move, become unavailable, or contain information that OWVAZ has not independently verified. Reliance, professional information, and emergencies OWVAZ provides civic information to help residents understand their communities and locate authoritative sources. Residents remain responsible for decisions they make based on information obtained from OWVAZ or from sources linked by OWVAZ. OWVAZ does not provide legal, financial, medical, or other professional advice. Information involving legal rights, deadlines, eligibility, emergency services, financial decisions, or other consequential matters should be confirmed with the responsible agency or a qualified professional when appropriate. OWVAZ is not an emergency service. For emergencies, use the appropriate official emergency service. No professional or official relationship Using OWVAZ does not create an attorney client, financial advisory, medical, fiduciary, governmental, or other professional relationship between a resident and OWVAZ or its operator. OWVAZ does not act on behalf of a government agency merely because it provides, summarizes, or links to government information. Corrections OWVAZ aims to correct factual errors when reliable information shows that a published statement is inaccurate or incomplete. Residents are encouraged to provide corrections and supporting sources through the Contact page. Responsibility for external changes and consequential reliance OWVAZ and its operator are not responsible for changes made by government agencies or other third parties after OWVAZ information was researched or published, or for an external website, document, service, or resource being changed, moved, or made unavailable. To the extent permitted by applicable law, OWVAZ and its operator are not responsible for losses resulting from a person's failure to verify time sensitive or consequential information with the responsible authoritative source when such verification is appropriate.

records.title: Privacy
records.summary: How Our West Valley AZ protects resident privacy.
records.text: Privacy How Our West Valley AZ protects resident privacy. Our West Valley AZ is designed around a simple privacy principle: residents should be able to access civic information without being tracked, profiled, or required to identify themselves to OWVAZ. Last updated: September 23, 2026. What OWVAZ does not use The OWVAZ website is designed without: resident accounts advertising networks behavioral analytics tracking pixels browser or device fingerprinting third party social trackers third party analytics scripts third party advertising scripts persistent browser storage for tracking or profiling OWVAZ does not sell resident information or use the website to build advertising, behavioral, or personal profiles of visitors. Cookies and browser storage The current OWVAZ site code does not set cookies and does not use localStorage, sessionStorage, or IndexedDB to identify, track, or profile residents. If a future feature requires cookies or persistent browser storage, its privacy impact must be evaluated before that feature is added and this page must be updated when appropriate. Search privacy OWVAZ search is designed to operate in the resident's browser. When a resident searches OWVAZ, the site loads static OWVAZ search index data from the same website and performs the search locally in the browser. The search form does not submit the resident's search terms to OWVAZ, a search engine, an analytics provider, or another third party search service. Loading a search index is a normal request for a static website file. The resident's typed search term is not included in that request. Contact form and information residents submit Residents can browse OWVAZ without creating an account or identifying themselves to OWVAZ. Using the contact form is optional. The contact form asks visitors to select a topic and enter a message. Depending on the topic, it may also ask for a city or an OWVAZ page address. Visitors submitting a general question can request a response; an email address is required only when they select that option. The form does not require a name. Please avoid including sensitive personal information in a message. When a visitor selects Send message , the form sends the submitted information to Web3Forms, a third party form processing service, for delivery to OWVAZ. Web3Forms may also receive technical information associated with the request, such as an IP address. Not providing a name or email address does not make a contact form submission anonymous. OWVAZ receives messages in its contact mailbox and uses them to review questions, reported website issues, proposed corrections, and other suggestions. Messages and related correspondence may be retained while an inquiry is addressed or a correction is reviewed. OWVAZ does not currently publish a fixed deletion schedule for contact messages. If a submission leads to a website correction, OWVAZ may independently verify and cite a relevant public source. OWVAZ does not ordinarily publish the sender's message, email address, or other contact details as part of that update. OWVAZ does not sell contact form submissions or use them to build advertising or behavioral profiles. Web3Forms processes submissions under its own privacy practices, including any applicable technical logging and retention. OWVAZ cannot guarantee deletion of information already processed or retained by that provider. Review Web3Forms' privacy information before submitting a message: https://web3forms.com/privacy To ask about information you previously submitted, or to request deletion of a message from OWVAZ's contact mailbox, use the contact form and select a general question. Provide enough information for OWVAZ to locate the message, but do not include sensitive personal information. OWVAZ may need to verify that a request relates to your own submission and cannot promise removal of copies held by third party services or already included in correspondence outside its control. External links OWVAZ links to official government agencies, public meeting systems, utilities, public documents, and other external sources. Following one of those links takes the resident to a website that OWVAZ does not operate or control. That external site may have its own cookies, analytics, logging, privacy practices, or terms. OWVAZ does not treat a link to an external website as permission for that site to track residents through OWVAZ. External resources are linked rather than automatically embedded whenever practical so residents can choose whether to visit them. Website requests and infrastructure Like any website, OWVAZ must receive a network request in order to send a requested page or file to a visitor's browser. That request can inherently include technical information needed for normal Internet communication, such as an IP address and basic request information. OWVAZ does not intend to use website infrastructure to track or profile residents. OWVAZ's production website is delivered through Cloudflare Pages and related network infrastructure. Cloudflare and other infrastructure providers may process technical request information as needed to deliver the website, maintain security, and operate their services. OWVAZ does not claim that infrastructure level logs do not exist or that every provider follows the same retention practices. The contact form involves an additional service, Web3Forms, as described above. Merely browsing OWVAZ does not submit a contact form message to Web3Forms. Privacy by design Privacy is treated as a design constraint rather than an optional feature. New analytics, tracking, advertising, profiling, third party embeds, or similar technologies are not assumed to be acceptable merely because they are common on other websites. If OWVAZ considers adding a feature that changes how resident information is handled, its purpose and privacy impact should be evaluated first. Changes to this privacy information OWVAZ's privacy practices and this page should be reviewed when a material change affects how resident or visitor information is handled. If OWVAZ adds a feature, service, or production technology that materially changes the privacy practices described here, this page should be updated to reflect that change.

records.title: Police Surveillance Technology
records.summary: Documented Avondale Police Department license plate readers, drones, body-worn cameras, and regional data-sharing systems.
records.text: Police Surveillance Technology Documented Avondale Police Department license plate readers, drones, body-worn cameras, and regional data-sharing systems. {{ }} OWVAZ is still gathering and verifying surveillance related records for this city. This page may not yet include newer records from recent fiscal years, contracts, purchases, vendor details, deployment status, or policy documents. It should be read as a working research page, not a complete inventory. {{ }} Avondale Police Department records document several technologies used to collect, search, share, or review information for law enforcement purposes. These include license plate reader cameras, police drones, body worn cameras, and regional data sharing systems. This page separates what City records currently document from proposals or details that have not yet been verified . {{ }} License plate readers Current system documented by the City The FY2027 City Manager's Recommended Budget states that Avondale Police Department operates 15 license plate reader (LPR) cameras throughout the city . The document says officers and dispatchers use the cameras to identify and query vehicles associated with crimes and calls for service. It also states that the camera database allows personnel to search for vehicles through cameras shared by more than 140 law enforcement agencies nationwide . The City describes real time alerts associated with categories including missing persons, vehicles used in felonies, stolen vehicles, stolen license plates, and other law enforcement alerts. Proposed FY2027 expansion The FY2027 recommended budget requested 58 additional license plate reader cameras . The stated purpose was to increase the number of cameras to provide citywide coverage in areas where cameras were not already present . The request was: $239,000 ongoing $0 one time $239,000 total annual request The FY2027 tentative budget continued to list the same 58 camera request and amount. Earlier LPR history Avondale's documented use of license plate reader technology predates the current program. A historical City budget describes implementation and training for an LPR system around 2008. The document says external cameras could read and store license plates and reports that approximately 50,000 plates had been collected during an early deployment period. The FY2023 final budget later reported that the Police Department had launched a license plate reader program and used it to identify two stolen vehicles. Because older City records already document LPR use, OWVAZ does not interpret the FY2023 wording as evidence that FY2023 was Avondale's first ever use of license plate readers. The FY2025 final budget also describes testing cameras functioning as license plate readers at intersections. The City says these cameras capture an image of vehicles passing through an intersection and can notify police when a vehicle of interest passes a monitored location. Police drones Avondale had an established police drone program before the FY2027 budget cycle. The FY2022 final budget documents a new drone program and says seven staff members were trained as licensed drone pilots. The FY2023 final budget reports that two additional drones were added. By the FY2027 recommended budget, the Police Department described a program consisting of 16 drones assigned to officers who had completed FAA training and received drone pilot licenses. Drone as First Responder The FY2027 recommended budget describes a proposed Drone as First Responder (DFR) model. The City's description involves a drone stored in an enclosed rooftop docking station that could be deployed by trained personnel to calls for service. The document says the system could provide information to responding officers before or during their arrival. The FY2027 supplemental request summary lists a $120,000 one time Public Safety Drone Program request. Body worn cameras Avondale Police Department's command staff page explicitly refers to an Axon Body Worn Camera Program . This establishes Axon in connection with Avondale's body worn camera program. It does not establish that Axon supplies Avondale's license plate readers or drone systems. FY2027 budget materials also contain a separate $25,000 ongoing request for body worn camera redaction software . Regional and interagency data sharing The FY2026 final budget reports that Avondale assigned one full time dispatcher to the West Valley Real Time Crime Center . Separately, the FY2027 recommended budget describes a Police Data Sharing request of: $75,000 ongoing $28,000 one time $103,000 total The City describes the proposed system as a nationwide data integration platform intended to combine otherwise separate law enforcement records into a searchable system and support interagency information sharing. OWVAZ does not currently treat the Police Data Sharing system, the West Valley Real Time Crime Center, and the 140 plus agency LPR camera database as the same system. The public records establish these facts separately. {{ }} What the public record does not yet show The earlier 58 camera LPR request and the final budget's State RICO funding assignment are both documented at $239,000 . The matching amounts do not, by themselves, establish that the final State RICO funding paid for the earlier 58 camera request. Public records reviewed by OWVAZ do not yet establish the following details: the vendor operating or supplying Avondale's current LPR network, the contract or purchase order for the current LPR system, the procurement vehicle for the proposed 58 camera expansion, the precise retention period for LPR records, the City's detailed LPR access and audit policy, the formal data sharing agreement governing the LPR network, the vendor for the proposed DFR system, the final deployment status of the 58 camera expansion, the final deployment status of DFR, or the exact vendor or product behind the FY2027 Police Data Sharing request. These details will remain unidentified unless supported by additional public records.

records.title: Proposition 418: Public Safety Bond
records.summary: What Avondale Proposition 418 would authorize, what the published materials say, and where surveillance-related budget questions remain separate from the bond language.
records.text: Proposition 418: Public Safety Bond What Avondale Proposition 418 would authorize, what the published materials say, and where surveillance-related budget questions remain separate from the bond language. What a yes or no vote means {{ }} {{ }} Authorizes the public safety bond. Authorizes Avondale to issue and sell up to $55,000,000 in general obligation bonds. The published ballot language says the bonds would fund public safety projects, including fire, emergency, police, training, and City Court facilities and improvements. The ballot language includes design, construction, reconstruction, improvement, repair, renovation, equipment, land acquisition, legal, financial, consulting, and related costs. The bonds would be repaid with secondary property taxes. {{ }} {{ }} Does not authorize the proposed public safety bond. The proposed $55,000,000 bond authorization would not be approved. Avondale would not receive this voter authorization to issue and sell the proposed general obligation bonds. The proposed bond funded public safety and court projects would need to be delayed, scaled back, postponed, or funded another way. {{ }} {{ }} {{ }} {{ }} Up to $55 million in general obligation bonds. {{ }} {{ }} Published materials describe public safety facility improvements, training facilities, a fire/police substation, public safety headquarters, a police firearms training facility, main police station expansion, and City Court office expansion. {{ }} {{ }} The ballot language says the bonds would be repaid with secondary property taxes. {{ }} {{ }} No specific reference to Flock, ALPRs, drones, surveillance software, or a real time crime center was found in the reviewed Prop 418 materials. {{ }} {{ }} No specific reference to data centers was found in the reviewed Prop 418 materials. {{ }} {{ }} {{ }} {{ }} Prop 418 is scheduled for Avondale voters in the November 2026 general election. {{ }} {{ }} The City would be authorized to issue the bonds in one or more series. The published FAQ says projects would be reviewed and prioritized by City Council and incorporated into the Capital Improvement Plan. {{ }} {{ }} Newer research update OWVAZ reviewed additional 2025–2026 public materials after this page was first drafted. Those records add useful context, but they do not change the core conclusion of this page. The newer records indicate that Proposition 418 is closely related to Avondale’s earlier 2025 public safety bond question, Proposition 405. Prop 405 also sought up to $55 million in general obligation bond authority for public safety projects. A 2026 city release states that City Council later placed Proposition 418 on the November 3, 2026 ballot for public safety and court related infrastructure. The 2026 city release describes proposed uses more broadly than the short public project list. It refers to fire stations and training facilities, public safety and court facilities, equipment, technology and communication systems, land acquisition, and site improvements. That broader language matters because it may leave the City with discretion to fund public safety capital items that fit within the final voter approved purpose. The recurring public facing project list remains facilities heavy: Southern Avondale / Alamar fire police substation New public safety headquarters or public safety operations facility Police firearms training facility Main police station expansion City Court expansion or office expansion The newer review also identified several related capital projects in recent Avondale budget and capital improvement records, including the Southern Avondale / Alamar fire police station, City Court expansion, training tower, Police Communications Bureau remodel, Regional Wireless Cooperative tower, K 9 training facility, assessment of existing public safety buildings, and additional communications work. Some of these may fit within the broader public safety/court/communications categories, but the records reviewed so far do not establish exactly which projects would be paid with Prop 418 bond proceeds rather than other funding sources. Importantly, the additional research still found no direct public record tying Proposition 418 specifically to Flock cameras, automated license plate readers, drones, a real time crime center, facial recognition, gunshot detection, or general surveillance expansion. The closest potentially relevant wording is the broad reference to equipment, technology, and communication systems. That language supports public questions about scope and oversight, but it is not the same as a documented surveillance funding line. The biggest missing source is still the official 2026 Proposition 418 publicity pamphlet and final ballot language. That document should be preserved and reviewed once available because it will define the final voter facing purpose and disclosure language for the bond. Why Proposition 418 is on the ballot Proposition 418 asks Avondale voters whether to authorize up to $55 million in general obligation bonds for public safety projects. The published support materials describe the proposal as funding for public safety facility improvement projects and training facilities. Listed projects include a new fire/police substation, a new public safety headquarters, a police firearms training facility, main police station expansion, and City Court office expansion. The City's published FAQ says the bond program is intended to fund projects over the next 20 years. If approved, the projects would be reviewed and prioritized by Avondale City Council and incorporated into the City's Capital Improvement Plan. What Proposition 418 would change Approval would authorize Avondale to issue and sell the proposed general obligation bonds. The ballot language describes the purpose as public safety projects, including: Designing, acquiring, equipping, and constructing fire, emergency, and police facilities for public safety and training. Designing, acquiring, and constructing City Court facilities and improvements. Paying related costs, including equipment, land acquisition or interests in land, legal costs, financial costs, consulting costs, and other associated costs. The ballot language says the bonds may have principal payable not later than 25 years from the date of issuance of each series. Financial figures {{ }} {{ }} Maximum principal amount of general obligation bonds described in the published ballot language. {{ }} {{ }} The ballot language says bond principal may be payable not later than 25 years from the date of issuance of each series. {{ }} {{ }} The published FAQ says combined property taxes for every $100,000 of assessed property valuation are expected to remain stable at about this amount, while also noting that projected property values and future bond issuance plans are subject to change. {{ }} {{ }} The ballot language says the bonds would be general obligation bonds and would be repaid with secondary property taxes. The FAQ states that the City expects the combined property tax rate to remain stable because new bonds would be issued as older bonds are retired. The FAQ also notes that the bonds would be payable from a property tax without limitation as to rate or amount. Surveillance and data center questions The reviewed Prop 418 materials do not specifically name data centers, Flock Safety, automated license plate readers, drones, surveillance software, or a real time crime center. That does not mean the public has no technology questions to ask. The ballot language is broader than buildings alone because it includes equipping public safety facilities and paying equipment related and associated costs. This matters because Avondale's separate police surveillance records document license plate readers, police drones, body worn cameras, and regional law enforcement data sharing systems. Those records are part of Avondale's broader public safety budget picture, but they are not the same thing as a direct Prop 418 funding line. A clear public question is whether any Prop 418 bond money could be used for surveillance related infrastructure, data systems, camera infrastructure, communications systems, or technology purchases. Another question is whether existing or proposed surveillance spending could be reduced or redirected before asking voters to authorize additional public safety debt. See also: Avondale Police Surveillance Technology. Timeline 2025 A prior Avondale public safety bond question was presented to voters. 2026 Avondale published materials for Proposition 418, a public safety bond question seeking authorization for up to $55 million in general obligation bonds. November 3, 2026 Proposition 418 is scheduled to appear before Avondale voters. After voter approval, if approved The published FAQ says projects would be reviewed and prioritized by Avondale City Council and incorporated into the Capital Improvement Plan.

records.title: Police Surveillance Technology
records.summary: Documented Tolleson license plate reader deployment and ALPR and drone-related budget records.
records.text: Police Surveillance Technology Documented Tolleson license plate reader deployment and ALPR and drone-related budget records. {{ }} OWVAZ is still gathering and verifying surveillance related records for this city. This page may not yet include newer records from recent fiscal years, contracts, purchases, vendor details, deployment status, or policy documents. It should be read as a working research page, not a complete inventory. {{ }} {{ }} Tolleson City records document the placement of license plate readers and budget allocations for automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras and drone related programs. This page distinguishes documented deployment from budgeted projects and identifies details that the reviewed records do not establish. License plate readers Documented FY2020 deployment Tolleson's FY2020 Comprehensive Annual Financial Report states that license plate readers were strategically placed throughout the city during fiscal year 2020. The report does not identify the manufacturer, number of readers, precise installation dates or locations, or whether the same equipment remains in operation. FY2021 and FY2022 budget entries Fiscal year City budget description Budget allocation : FY2021 ALPR Cameras (License Plate Project) $50,000 FY2022 ALPR Cameras (License Plate Project) $60,000 Each fiscal year's Capital Improvement Plan and adopted budget repeat the same project entry. They are not separate allocations within that year. These entries document budgeted amounts, not confirmed purchases or expenditures . The reviewed records do not establish whether the FY2022 entry represented additional equipment, a continuation of the earlier project, or replacement equipment. Drone budget history Tolleson budget documents separately identify a Drone Project, a FEMA Drone Program (FEMA stands for Federal Emergency Management Agency), and Public Safety Police drone entries. The reviewed records do not establish the FEMA Drone Program’s funding source, operational purpose, or relationship to the separately listed police drone entries. Fiscal year Budget description Budget allocation : FY2020 Drone Project $10,000 FY2023 FEMA Drone Program $167,000 FY2025 FEMA Drone Program equipment $63,620 FY2026 FEMA Drone Program equipment $63,620 FY2026 Public Safety Police – Drone $35,000 FY2027 FEMA Drone Program equipment $63,620 FY2027 Public Safety Police – First Responder Drone $65,000 FY2027 Public Safety Police – Drone $40,000 These are budget entries, not confirmed purchases or cumulative spending. Repeated FEMA Drone Program entries across fiscal years should not be added together as though they represent separate purchases. The FEMA Drone Program and police drone entries are presented separately because the reviewed records do not establish that they describe the same equipment or program. {{ }} What the reviewed records do not establish The reviewed records do not establish: Tolleson's current ALPR camera count or complete equipment inventory. The manufacturer or vendor of the FY2020 ALPR equipment or later ALPR projects. Whether the FY2021 and FY2022 ALPR allocations resulted in purchases, expansion, or replacement. The complete actual expenditure history for ALPR and drone equipment. The current ALPR data retention period, access controls, or data sharing arrangements. The current operational status, equipment count, or vendor of the drone related programs. An unidentified detail should not be interpreted as evidence that the equipment, policy, or arrangement does not exist.

records.title: Proposition 416: Permanent Base Adjustment
records.summary: What Tolleson Proposition 416 would change about the City's state constitutional expenditure limitation.
records.text: Proposition 416: Permanent Base Adjustment What Tolleson Proposition 416 would change about the City's state constitutional expenditure limitation. What a yes or no vote means {{ }} {{ }} Approves the permanent base adjustment. Increases Tolleson's 1979 80 expenditure base by $39,033,506 . Establishes a new expenditure base of $40,000,000 . The base continues to be adjusted annually for population growth and inflation. The adjusted expenditure limitation begins in fiscal year 2028 . According to the City's ballot language, Tolleson would be permitted to spend revenues it already receives, subject to the annual budget process. {{ }} {{ }} Does not approve the permanent base adjustment. The proposed $39,033,506 adjustment is not made. According to the City, Tolleson would continue operating under its current expenditure limitation method for two additional years . If the City does not obtain an alternative expenditure limitation in 2028 , it would be subject to the state imposed expenditure limit. Under that limit, the City could not spend revenues beyond the amount permitted by the state formula. {{ }} {{ }} {{ }} {{ }} According to the City, no. Proposition 416 does not increase or create property or sales taxes. {{ }} {{ }} No. The measure changes how much revenue the City is permitted to spend; it does not generate new revenue. {{ }} {{ }} Yes. If approved, the base adjustment remains in effect permanently and continues to be adjusted for population growth and inflation. {{ }} {{ }} Fiscal year 2028, if approved. {{ }} {{ }} Lawful municipal purposes including public safety, water and wastewater services, streets and infrastructure, parks and recreation, public works, and other City services. Actual spending decisions would continue through the annual budget process. {{ }} {{ }} {{ }} {{ }} Deadline to register for the November general election. {{ }} {{ }} Last day to request an early ballot. {{ }} {{ }} Polls are open from 6:00 AM to 7:00 PM . {{ }} {{ }} The adjusted expenditure limitation would begin. {{ }} {{ }} Why Proposition 416 is on the ballot Arizona's expenditure limit formula uses municipal spending from fiscal year 1979 80 as its base and adjusts that amount for population growth and inflation. Changing the base requires voter approval. Tolleson currently operates under a voter approved Home Rule expenditure limitation. According to the City's FAQ, the current Home Rule was approved in 2024 and must be approved by voters every four years. A permanent base adjustment instead changes the base used by the state expenditure limit formula and, once approved, remains in effect permanently. The Tolleson City Council submitted the permanent base adjustment to voters through Resolution No. 2635. The City states that it is seeking the adjustment because Tolleson's population and service demands have grown while the state formula continues to use fiscal year 1979 80 as its baseline. What Proposition 416 would change Arizona's state expenditure limitation for cities and towns uses a base tied to fiscal year 1979 80 and adjusts that amount over time for population growth and inflation. Proposition 416 would permanently increase Tolleson's 1979 80 expenditure base by $39,033,506, resulting in a new base of $40,000,000. That $40 million figure is not Tolleson's annual budget and is not a proposed annual spending amount . It is the revised base that would be used in the constitutional expenditure limit calculation. The base would continue to be adjusted annually for population growth and inflation. If approved by voters in 2026, the adjusted expenditure limitation would take effect beginning in fiscal year 2028. Financial figures The City's Proposition 416 materials contain financial figures that represent different parts of the expenditure limit calculation. {{ }} {{ }} Proposed fiscal year 1979 80 expenditure base used in the state expenditure limit calculation. {{ }} {{ }} Approximate expenditure limitation published in the City's Proposition 416 FAQ. {{ }} {{ }} Approximate expenditure limitation published on the City's current Permanent Base Adjustment webpage. {{ }} {{ }} The two expenditure limit estimates apply to different fiscal years and should not be treated as competing figures for the same period. They also should not be confused with Tolleson's adopted annual budget. Tolleson's adopted fiscal year 2026 27 budget totals $247,153,697 . That budget is separate from the expenditure limitation, which determines how much revenue may be spent under the applicable constitutional framework. The City Council separately makes spending decisions through the annual budget process. Timeline April 15, 2026 The Tolleson City Council adopted Resolution No. 2635 to submit the Permanent Base Adjustment proposal to voters. June 17, 2026 The City published its Proposition 416 Permanent Base Adjustment and Call for Arguments notice. August 5, 2026 Deadline identified by the City for submitting ballot arguments. November 3, 2026 Proposition 416 is scheduled to appear on Tolleson's general election ballot. Fiscal year 2028 If approved, the adjusted expenditure limitation would take effect beginning in this fiscal year.

records.title: Proposition 434: Home Rule Option
records.summary: What Tolleson Proposition 434 proposed about the City's local alternative expenditure limitation.
records.text: Proposition 434: Home Rule Option What Tolleson Proposition 434 proposed about the City's local alternative expenditure limitation. What a yes or no vote meant {{ }} {{ }} Continued the Home Rule Option Local Alternative Expenditure Limitation. Continued the City's alternative expenditure limitation for four years. Allowed the City to establish its expenditure limitation based on its revenues and community needs rather than the state imposed formula. Allowed expenditures approved through the City's annual budget process for services including Police, Fire, Wastewater and Water. The City stated that continuing Home Rule would not change the property tax or sales tax it already collected. {{ }} {{ }} Did not continue the Home Rule Option. The City would have operated under the state imposed expenditure limitation. The City stated that this would have reduced the amount it could spend under the state formula. The City's October 2020 FAQ estimated the state imposed FY2020 21 limitation at $16,574,623, compared with a FY2019 20 budget of $76,796,734. {{ }} {{ }} {{ }} {{ }} According to the City, no. Continuing Home Rule did not change the property tax or sales tax the City already collected. {{ }} {{ }} No. The measure concerned the amount of revenue the City could spend under its expenditure limitation. {{ }} {{ }} Four years. {{ }} {{ }} The City identified services including Police, Fire, Wastewater and Water. {{ }} {{ }} Proposition 434 was approved. The final official results recorded 1,784 YES votes and 275 NO votes. {{ }} {{ }} Why Proposition 434 was on the ballot Arizona's expenditure limitation system allows local voters to approve an alternative expenditure limitation known as Home Rule. The City stated that Tolleson's voters had previously approved Home Rule in 2016 and that the 2020 election was the next required approval. The City described Proposition 434 as a four year extension of the Home Rule Option Local Alternative Expenditure Limitation. What Proposition 434 would change Under the Home Rule Option, the City stated that it could determine its expenditures based on available revenue and community needs while continuing to operate under a balanced budget requirement. Without Home Rule, the City would have been subject to the state imposed expenditure limitation. The City stated that Home Rule did not authorize new taxes and did not change the property tax or sales tax it already collected. Financial figures {{ }} {{ }} The City's October 2020 FAQ identified an estimated state imposed expenditure limitation of $16,574,623 for fiscal year 2020 21. {{ }} {{ }} The City's October 2020 FAQ identified a FY2019 20 budget of $76,796,734. {{ }} {{ }} The figures above came from the City's 2020 Home Rule FAQ and applied to different fiscal years. The $16,574,623 figure was an estimate of the state imposed expenditure limitation, not the City's annual budget. Timeline 2016 Tolleson voters previously approved Home Rule, according to the City's 2020 FAQ. October 1, 2020 The City published information about Proposition 434 and the other two Tolleson propositions on the November general election ballot. November 3, 2020 Proposition 434 appeared on the City of Tolleson's general election ballot. November 13, 2020 Maricopa County's final official results recorded 1,784 YES votes and 275 NO votes for Proposition 434. Official Sources City of Tolleson, October 2020 election information and Home Rule FAQ. Maricopa County Elections, November 3, 2020 Final Official Summary Report.

records.title: Proposition 435: General Obligation Bonds
records.summary: What Tolleson Proposition 435 proposed for parks and recreation projects and how the bonds would be repaid.
records.text: Proposition 435: General Obligation Bonds What Tolleson Proposition 435 proposed for parks and recreation projects and how the bonds would be repaid. What a yes or no vote meant {{ }} {{ }} Approved the issuance of general obligation bonds. Authorized up to $21,000,000 in general obligation bonds. The City stated that the bonds would fund parks and recreation projects, including an aquatic facility. The bonds would be repaid through secondary property taxes. The City stated that issuing the bonds would result in a property tax increase sufficient to pay annual debt service. {{ }} {{ }} Did not authorize the proposed general obligation bonds. The proposed $21 million bond issuance would not have been authorized. The proposed parks and recreation projects would not have received funding from these bonds. The proposed secondary property tax debt service associated with the bonds would not have been established. {{ }} {{ }} {{ }} {{ }} $21 million. {{ }} {{ }} The City identified parks and recreation projects, including an aquatic facility. {{ }} {{ }} The City stated that they would be repaid through secondary property taxes. {{ }} {{ }} Yes. The City's ballot description stated that issuing the bonds would result in a property tax increase sufficient to pay annual debt service. {{ }} {{ }} Proposition 435 was approved. The final official results recorded 1,334 YES votes and 744 NO votes. {{ }} {{ }} Why Proposition 435 was on the ballot Proposition 435 asked Tolleson voters to authorize the issuance and sale of $21 million in general obligation bonds. The City described the proposed bonds as funding for parks and recreation projects, including an aquatic facility. What Proposition 435 would change Approval would authorize the City to issue the proposed general obligation bonds. The City's October 2020 election information stated that the bonds would be repaid through secondary property taxes and that issuing the bonds would result in a property tax increase sufficient to pay the annual debt service. Financial figures {{ }} {{ }} The amount of general obligation bonds described in the City's ballot information. {{ }} {{ }} The City source reviewed for Proposition 435 identifies the bond amount and proposed projects but does not establish a single repayment term in the material used for this page. {{ }} {{ }} The City identified secondary property taxes as the repayment source and stated that issuing the bonds would result in a property tax increase sufficient to pay annual debt service. Timeline October 1, 2020 The City published information about Proposition 435 and the other two Tolleson propositions on the November general election ballot. November 3, 2020 Proposition 435 appeared on the City of Tolleson's general election ballot. November 13, 2020 Maricopa County's final official results recorded 1,334 YES votes and 744 NO votes for Proposition 435. Official Sources City of Tolleson, October 2020 election information. City of Tolleson, 2020 General Obligation Bond Election materials referenced by the City. Maricopa County Elections, November 3, 2020 Final Official Summary Report.

records.title: Proposition 436: Southwest Gas Corporation Franchise
records.summary: What Tolleson Proposition 436 proposed regarding Southwest Gas Corporation's use of City rights-of-way.
records.text: Proposition 436: Southwest Gas Corporation Franchise What Tolleson Proposition 436 proposed regarding Southwest Gas Corporation's use of City rights-of-way. What a yes or no vote meant {{ }} {{ }} Approved the Southwest Gas Corporation franchise. Authorized a franchise agreement with Southwest Gas Corporation. Allowed use of City rights of way for gas utility purposes. The City described the proposed term as up to 25 years . The October 2020 City notice identified the term as beginning November 4, 2020 and ending November 4, 2045. {{ }} {{ }} Did not approve the proposed franchise. The proposed franchise agreement would not have been approved through Proposition 436. Southwest Gas would not have received the proposed franchise authorization described in the ballot materials. {{ }} {{ }} {{ }} {{ }} Use of City rights of way for gas utility purposes. {{ }} {{ }} Up to 25 years, from November 4, 2020 through November 4, 2045, according to the City's October 2020 election notice. {{ }} {{ }} Southwest Gas Corporation. {{ }} {{ }} No. Proposition 436 concerned a utility franchise agreement and use of City rights of way. {{ }} {{ }} Proposition 436 was approved. The final official results recorded 1,602 YES votes and 413 NO votes. {{ }} {{ }} Why Proposition 436 was on the ballot Proposition 436 concerned renewal of a franchise agreement with Southwest Gas Corporation. The City described the franchise as authorization for the use of City rights of way for gas utility purposes. What Proposition 436 would change The proposed franchise would provide Southwest Gas Corporation with the franchise authorization described by the City for use of City rights of way. The City's October 2020 election notice described the agreement as a 25 year term beginning November 4, 2020 and ending November 4, 2045. Key terms {{ }} {{ }} The City described the proposed franchise as having a term of up to 25 years. {{ }} {{ }} The City's October 2020 notice identified November 4, 2020 as the beginning of the proposed franchise term. {{ }} {{ }} The City's October 2020 notice identified November 4, 2045 as the end of the proposed franchise term. {{ }} {{ }} Timeline October 1, 2020 The City published information about Proposition 436 and the other two Tolleson propositions on the November general election ballot. November 3, 2020 Proposition 436 appeared on the City of Tolleson's general election ballot. November 4, 2020 The City identified this date as the beginning of the proposed 25 year franchise term. November 13, 2020 Maricopa County's final official results recorded 1,602 YES votes and 413 NO votes for Proposition 436. November 4, 2045 The City identified this date as the end of the proposed franchise term. Official Sources City of Tolleson, October 2020 election information.
